newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees in Zaire are dying of thirst.
newsitem.headline: Refugees in Zaire are dying of thirst.

text.p: Rwandan refugees are dying of thirst in the harsh mountains of east Zaire, U.N. officials said on Thursday quoting some of the first eyewitness accounts from the war-ravaged region.
Refugees arriving in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma told U.N. officials of many deaths in the waterless, volcanic mountains north of Lake Kivu.

"They said they saw people dying all around them due to lack of water on the escarpment above Kahindo and Katale camps. One man was sucking water out of tree roots," said Peter Kessler, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency in Nairobi.
European Union aid ministers met in Brussels on Thursday to try to define a joint approach to the deepening tragedy.
Humanitarian Aid Commissioner Emma Bonino said something had to be done urgently.
"My feeling is that it is not time any longer for political reports, a strong call has to come from this meeting," Bonino told Reuters.
She wants the international community to open safe corridors for food deliveries and the return of refugees to Rwanda.
Aid agencies have been sounding the alarm over the 1.2 million Hutu refugees in Zaire for weeks, but international efforts to help have so far faded before the sheer complexities of the task.
The part of east Zaire where the refugees are dying is no longer in government hands.
It is held by an extraordinary medley of armies and militias acting out tribal and political rivalries, fuelled by land hunger, which threaten to tear Zaire apart.
Most of the refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled into Zaire after the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and other victims in Rwanda in 1994.
The rebels who captured much of eastern Zaire in a two-week lightning offensive include Tutsis, the Hutus' foes.

Many refugees fear that if they return to their countries of origin, Rwanda and Burundi, they will be slaughtered by Tutsi-led armies. Only about 2,000 Rwandan refugees have returned to Rwanda in recent weeks, U.N. officials say.
Thousands of Zairean refugees have fled the mayhem and many have arrived wounded or exhausted in neighbouring countries.
Wendy Driscoll, a spokeswoman for CARE International in Nairobi, said the agency had reports of a 14 percent severe malnutrition rate among refugee children under five arriving in Tanzania.
"That's very, very high for such a situation," she said.
Information on the refugees has been sketchy and there are still big question marks over what can be done to help them.
On Wednesday Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko gave his support for an international intervention force to go into eastern Zaire on a humanitarian mission.
Mobutu has warmed to a French plan for an intervention force, hoping perhaps that it might be a way to reassert his control in eastern Zaire.

Providing military help for Mobutu is not on the agenda of the United States, which has long barred him from its soil over his human rights record. Washington complains France is not being clear about what it envisages.
U.S. officials said the proposals were changing daily, creating confusion. Questions about what is a safe corridor and what troops might be involved have not been answered, they said.
On Wednesday the State Department said that Washington was leaning toward backing the proposed force but would not itself contribute ground troops.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette has voiced disappointment at the lack of response, blaming it on "the international community's spinelessness".
Kenya, which hosted an eight-nation summit on the Zaire crisis last Tuesday, welcomed Mobutu's support for an international force.
"That is a very important statement," Kenyan foreign ministry spokesman David Kikaya told Reuters on Thursday.
But the slow pace of diplomacy on such a complex issue means countless refugees are dying daily before any effective help is provided.
The Organisation of African Unity plans no further meeting on east Zaire until next Monday. Only France, Spain and Ethiopia have promised troops for an intervention force for eastern Zaire.
In Goma, the biggest city under rebel control, rebels on Thursday supervised the orderly distribution of oil, salt, biscuits and maize from a United Nations warehouse. Food in Goma is now scarce.
